--- title: "Publication Bias Diagnostics" subtitle: "Small-Study Effects and Time-Lag Bias in Mate-Choice Copying (MCC) Meta-Analyses" author: "Eduardo S. A. Santos & Collaborators" date: today bibliography: ../../references.bib format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 theme: cosmo --- ## Introduction & Methodology Publication bias is a critical threat to the validity of meta-analytic syntheses. If studies with statistically non-significant or small effects are systematically omitted from the literature, the pooled meta-analytic summary will be biased upward. To thoroughly evaluate the presence of publication bias and report-level selection in our Mate-Choice Copying (MCC) dataset, we employ three complementary diagnostic approaches, keeping the exact multilevel modeling logic (e.g., nested random intercepts and taxonomy control) used in our main overall effect calculations: 1. **Visual Inspection (Funnel Plots):** We plot effect size estimates against their precision (inverse of the standard error, $1/\text{SE}$) to check for visual asymmetry around the overall mean estimate. 2. **Egger's Meta-Regression (Small-Study Effects):** We test whether study precision significantly moderates effect size. Following the recommendations of @nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022 and Stanley [-@stanleyMetaregressionAnalysisEconomics2012; -@stanleyMetaregressionApproximationsReduce2014], we implement a **two-step approach**: * We first fit the Egger regression with the standard error ($\text{SE} = \sqrt{v_i}$) as the moderator. The slope tests for small-study effects, and the intercept estimates the effect that a perfectly precise study ($\text{SE} = 0$) would report. * When that intercept is statistically significant — i.e., a genuine non-zero effect is likely present — the standard-error version is known to under-estimate the true effect. We therefore re-fit the regression with the sampling variance ($\text{V} = v_i$) as the moderator, which gives a less biased estimate of the bias-adjusted overall mean. 3. **Decline Effect / Time-Lag Bias:** We test whether effect sizes shrink over time by adding publication year (mean-centered) to our models while simultaneously controlling for study precision. 4. **Bias-Corrected Meta-Analytic Means (Method Comparison):** Finally, we estimate the *adjusted* overall mean under two complementary correction frameworks and compare them directly. The **current** approach follows @nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022: the intercept of a multilevel meta-regression on the sampling variance ($v_i$) is interpreted as the mean when sampling error is zero (i.e., an infinitely precise study). The **new** approach follows @yangRobustPointVariance2024: a *bias-robust* weighting scheme (a fixed-/common-effect GLS estimator that is less susceptible to selective reporting) is combined with **cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimation** to handle the non-independence of effect sizes within studies. We overlay both corrected means on an orchard plot using `orchaRd::pub_bias_plot()`. --- ## Data Loading and Alignment We read, clean, and align the new extractions and original datasets, extracting sample sizes and publication years to construct our precision and time-lag moderators. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Paths to datasets path_new <- here::here("data", "1_effect_size_calculation_pipeline", "Data Extraction Mate Choice Meta Analysis.xlsx") path_davies <- here::here("data", "original_meta_analyses_datasets", "Davies_et_al_2020_Final_data.xlsx") path_jones <- here::here("data", "original_meta_analyses_datasets", "Jones_DuVal_2019_data.CSV") # A. Read raw spreadsheets db_new_raw <- readxl::read_excel(path_new, sheet = "EduardoExtraction") db_davies_raw <- readxl::read_excel(path_davies, sheet = "Data") db_jones_raw <- readr::read_csv(path_jones) # A2. Species-name reconciliation + phylogenetic correlation matrices. # Ported verbatim from overall_effect.qmd so that every multilevel model in the # project shares one random-effects structure. The correlation matrices are # indexed by FULL species binomials; these maps reproduce the reconciliation in # scripts/2_phylogeny/build_phylogeny.R. recode_new <- c("Taeniopygia guttata castanotis" = "Taeniopygia guttata") recode_davies <- c("Schizocosa" = "Schizocosa ocreata") jones_binomial <- tibble::tribble( ~family, ~epithet, ~species_phylo, "Adrianichthyidae", "latipes", "Oryzias latipes", "Blenniidae", "nitidus", "Rhabdoblennius nitidus", "Gasterosteidae", "aculeatus", "Gasterosteus aculeatus", "Gobiidae", "minutu", "Pomatoschistus minutus", "Percidae", "olmstedi", "Etheostoma olmstedi", "Poeciliidae", "latipinna", "Poecilia latipinna", "Poeciliidae", "nigrofasciata", "Limia nigrofasciata", "Poeciliidae", "perugiae", "Limia perugiae", "Poeciliidae", "reticulata", "Poecilia reticulata", "Pomacentridae", "leucogaster", "Amblyglyphidodon leucogaster", "Lycosidae", "ocreata", "Schizocosa ocreata", "Estrildidae", "guttata", "Taeniopygia guttata", "Icteridae", "ater", "Molothrus ater", "Muscicapidae", "hypoleuca", "Ficedula hypoleuca", "Drosophilidae", "melanogaster", "Drosophila melanogaster", "Drosophilidae", "serrata", "Drosophila serrata", "Ocypodidae", "mjoebergi", "Uca mjoebergi" ) read_phylo <- function(f) { pth <- here::here("outputs", "2_phylogeny", f) if (file.exists(pth)) readRDS(pth) else NULL } phylo_cor_hedges <- read_phylo("phylo_cor_hedges_model.rds") phylo_cor_or <- read_phylo("phylo_cor_or_model.rds") # Helper: return the random-effects list, the R argument and a levels-cleaned # copy of the data, adding the phylogenetic term only when every species level # is present in the correlation matrix. Falls back with a warning otherwise, so # a missing phylogeny degrades the fit rather than breaking the render. phylo_terms <- function(dat, phylo_cor, phylo_var = "species_phylo") { base <- list(~ 1 | identifierStudyId, ~ 1 | identifierEffectSizeID, ~ 1 | taxonomySpecies) if (is.null(phylo_cor) || !phylo_var %in% colnames(dat)) { return(list(data = dat, random = base, R = NULL, used_phylo = FALSE)) } sp <- unique(as.character(dat[[phylo_var]])) missing_sp <- setdiff(sp, rownames(phylo_cor)) if (length(missing_sp) > 0) { warning("Phylogenetic random effect skipped (species absent from correlation matrix): ", paste(missing_sp, collapse = ", ")) return(list(data = dat, random = base, R = NULL, used_phylo = FALSE)) } dat[[phylo_var]] <- factor(as.character(dat[[phylo_var]])) list( data = dat, random = c(base, list(stats::as.formula(paste0("~ 1 | ", phylo_var)))), R = stats::setNames(list(phylo_cor[sp, sp, drop = FALSE]), phylo_var), used_phylo = TRUE ) } # B. Clean new extractions db_new <- db_new_raw %>% filter(is.na(RemoveFromDataset) | RemoveFromDataset != "Yes") %>% mutate( effectSizeCalculatedHedgesD = as.numeric(effectSizeCalculatedHedgesD), effectSizeCalculatedHedgesDVariance = as.numeric(effectSizeCalculatedHedgesDVariance), effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatio = as.numeric(effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatio), effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatioVariance = as.numeric(effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatioVariance), logOddsRatio = log(effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatio), logOddsRatioVariance = effectSizeCalculatedOddsRatioVariance, identifierStudyYear = as.numeric(identifierStudyYear), controlN = as.numeric(controlN), treatmentN = as.numeric(treatmentN), effectSizesampleSize = as.numeric(effectSizesampleSize) ) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1. Hedges' g Dataset Alignment (Continuous) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- hedges_new <- db_new %>% filter(!is.na(effectSizeCalculatedHedgesD), !is.na(effectSizeCalculatedHedgesDVariance)) %>% select( yi = effectSizeCalculatedHedgesD, vi = effectSizeCalculatedHedgesDVariance, identifierStudyId, identifierEffectSizeID, taxonomySpecies, Year = identifierStudyYear, controlN, treatmentN, totalN = effectSizesampleSize ) %>% mutate( identifierStudyId = as.character(identifierStudyId), identifierEffectSizeID = as.character(identifierEffectSizeID), species_phylo = dplyr::recode(str_squish(as.character(taxonomySpecies)), !!!recode_new), taxonomySpecies = str_to_lower(word(as.character(taxonomySpecies), -1)), Dataset_Source = "New Extraction (Santos)" ) hedges_davies <- db_davies_raw %>% mutate( Hedges_d_directional = as.numeric(Hedges_d_directional), Variance = as.numeric(Variance), Year = as.numeric(Year), N_control = as.numeric(N_control), N_treatment = as.numeric(N_treatment), Total_n_analysis = as.numeric(Total_n_analysis), .study_id = paste0(Author, " [", Study_no, "]") ) %>% filter(!is.na(Hedges_d_directional), !is.na(Variance), Variance > 0) %>% select( yi = Hedges_d_directional, vi = Variance, # Davies' own study identifier -- see the note in overall_effect.qmd: # keying on `Author` merges separate publications by the same authors. identifierStudyId = .study_id, identifierEffectSizeID = Effect_size_no, taxonomySpecies = Species_latin, Year, controlN = N_control, treatmentN = N_treatment, totalN = Total_n_analysis ) %>% mutate( identifierStudyId = as.character(identifierStudyId), identifierEffectSizeID = as.character(identifierEffectSizeID), species_phylo = dplyr::recode(str_squish(as.character(taxonomySpecies)), !!!recode_davies), taxonomySpecies = str_to_lower(word(as.character(taxonomySpecies), -1)), Dataset_Source = "Original (Davies 2020)" ) db_hedges <- bind_rows(hedges_new, hedges_davies) %>% mutate(across(c(identifierStudyId, taxonomySpecies, species_phylo, Dataset_Source), as.factor)) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2. Log Odds Ratio Dataset Alignment (Binary) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- or_new <- db_new %>% filter(!is.na(logOddsRatio), !is.na(logOddsRatioVariance)) %>% select( yi = logOddsRatio, vi = logOddsRatioVariance, identifierStudyId, identifierEffectSizeID, taxonomySpecies, Year = identifierStudyYear ) %>% mutate( identifierStudyId = as.character(identifierStudyId), identifierEffectSizeID = as.character(identifierEffectSizeID), species_phylo = dplyr::recode(str_squish(as.character(taxonomySpecies)), !!!recode_new), taxonomySpecies = str_to_lower(word(as.character(taxonomySpecies), -1)), Dataset_Source = "New Extraction (Santos)" ) or_jones <- db_jones_raw %>% filter(!is.na(lnOR), !is.na(VlnOR), VlnOR > 0) %>% mutate( family = str_squish(as.character(Family)), epithet = str_squish(as.character(Species)) ) %>% # Rebuild the full binomial (species_phylo) from Family + epithet left_join(jones_binomial, by = c("family", "epithet")) %>% select( yi = lnOR, vi = VlnOR, identifierStudyId = study, identifierEffectSizeID = study_Exp, taxonomySpecies = Species, species_phylo, Year = year ) %>% mutate( identifierStudyId = as.character(identifierStudyId), identifierEffectSizeID = as.character(identifierEffectSizeID), taxonomySpecies = str_to_lower(as.character(taxonomySpecies)), Dataset_Source = "Original (Jones & DuVal 2019)" ) # Sanity check: every Jones epithet should map to a full binomial if (any(is.na(or_jones$species_phylo))) { warning( "Unmapped Jones epithets (phylogeny): ", paste(unique(or_jones$taxonomySpecies[is.na(or_jones$species_phylo)]), collapse = ", ") ) } db_or <- bind_rows(or_new, or_jones) %>% mutate(across(c(identifierStudyId, taxonomySpecies, species_phylo, Dataset_Source), as.factor)) ``` ::: --- ## Study Inclusion & Exclusion {#sec-inclusion-pb} The following tables document which effect sizes from the new extraction are included in the meta-analytic models and which have been removed, with the reason for each exclusion. ### Excluded Effect Sizes ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Included Effect Sizes ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## Diagnostics by Effect Size Class ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Hedges' $g$ (Continuous outcomes) We fit multilevel models on the continuous combined dataset ($k = 227$) to run our diagnostics. #### 1. Baseline Model & Funnel Plot We run the intercept-only model to establish the global mean effect size and plot precision ($1/\text{SE}$) against the standardized residuals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Intercept-only model VCV_hedges <- metafor::vcalc(vi = vi, cluster = identifierStudyId, obs = identifierEffectSizeID, rho = 0.5, data = db_hedges) # Phylogenetic random effect (see phylo_terms() in the data-prep chunk). pt_db_hedges <- phylo_terms(db_hedges, phylo_cor_hedges) ma_hedges <- metafor::rma.mv( yi = yi, V = VCV_hedges, random = pt_db_hedges$random, R = pt_db_hedges$R, test = "t", dfs = "contain", method = "REML", sparse = TRUE, data = pt_db_hedges$data ) summary(ma_hedges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 227; method: REML) logLik Deviance AIC BIC AICc -257.9500 515.9000 525.9000 543.0026 526.1727 Variance Components: estim sqrt nlvls fixed factor R sigma^2.1 0.0525 0.2292 87 no identifierStudyId no sigma^2.2 0.3485 0.5904 227 no identifierEffectSizeID no sigma^2.3 0.0096 0.0981 31 no taxonomySpecies no sigma^2.4 0.0163 0.1276 30 no species_phylo yes Test for Heterogeneity: Q(df = 226) = 1389.2944, p-val < .0001 Model Results: estimate se tval df pval ci.lb ci.ub 0.4537 0.0994 4.5651 29 <.0001 0.2504 0.6570 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Extract BLUPs for random effects blups <- ranef(ma_hedges) study_ef <- blups$identifierStudyId$intrcpt[match(db_hedges$identifierStudyId, row.names(blups$identifierStudyId))] obs_ef <- blups$identifierEffectSizeID$intrcpt[match(db_hedges$identifierEffectSizeID, row.names(blups$identifierEffectSizeID))] spec_ef <- blups$taxonomySpecies$intrcpt[match(db_hedges$taxonomySpecies, row.names(blups$taxonomySpecies))] # Handle any missing values by replacing with 0 study_ef[is.na(study_ef)] <- 0 obs_ef[is.na(obs_ef)] <- 0 spec_ef[is.na(spec_ef)] <- 0 # Marginal residuals: observed - fixed-effect prediction resid_marg <- db_hedges$yi - predict(ma_hedges)[[1]] # Conditional residuals: observed - fixed - random intercepts (study, obs, species) resid_cond <- db_hedges$yi - (predict(ma_hedges)[[1]] + study_ef + obs_ef + spec_ef) # Side-by-side funnel plots of marginal vs. conditional residuals, # with (a)/(b) panel tags. Drawn on-screen and saved to a manuscript PDF. draw_funnels(resid_marg, resid_cond, db_hedges$vi) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](publication_bias_files/figure-html/hedges_baseline_and_funnel-1.png){width=1152} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} save_base_pdf( "funnel_hedges", function() draw_funnels(resid_marg, resid_cond, db_hedges$vi) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` quartz_off_screen 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Reading the funnel plots"} Both panels plot each effect size against its precision ($1/\text{SE}$), but differ in what is removed before plotting: * **(a) Marginal residuals** are the deviations of each observed effect from the *fixed-effect (intercept) prediction* — the pooled mean — so they still carry all of the random-effects heterogeneity (between-study, between-effect-size, and between-species). Asymmetry here — a shortage of small, imprecise studies on one side of the funnel — is the classic visual signature of small-study and publication bias. Because genuine heterogeneity can mimic or exaggerate that asymmetry, apparent gaps in (a) should be read cautiously and confirmed against the formal Egger's regression below. * **(b) Conditional residuals** additionally subtract the estimated random intercepts (study, effect-size, and species BLUPs), so the heterogeneity captured by the multilevel structure is partialled out. A symmetric, evenly-filled funnel here means that once the nesting is accounted for there is little precision-related asymmetry left — i.e., the asymmetry seen in (a) is largely explained by the modelled random effects rather than by selective reporting. Any asymmetry that *persists* in (b) is the more credible visual indication of true small-study effects. ::: #### 2. Egger's Meta-Regression (Small-Study Effects) To perform Egger's regression on Hedges' $g$, we follow the two-step framework recommended by @nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022 and Stanley [-@stanleyMetaregressionAnalysisEconomics2012; -@stanleyMetaregressionApproximationsReduce2014]. We use the sampling standard error ($\text{SE} = \sqrt{v_i}$) as our precision proxy. If this moderator is statistically significant ($p < 0.05$), it indicates a significant small-study effect (larger standard errors / smaller sample sizes associated with larger effect magnitudes). When the intercept of the standard-error model is significant (a genuine non-zero effect is likely present), that intercept tends to under-estimate the true effect. We therefore apply the second step: re-fit Egger's regression with the sampling variance ($\text{V} = \text{vi}$) as the moderator, whose intercept gives a less biased estimate of the bias-adjusted overall mean. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate standard error precision proxy db_hedges_egger <- db_hedges %>% mutate(se = sqrt(vi)) %>% filter(!is.na(se)) # Re-estimate VCV on this subset VCV_hedges_egger <- metafor::vcalc(vi = vi, cluster = identifierStudyId, obs = identifierEffectSizeID, rho = 0.5, data = db_hedges_egger) # Phylogenetic random effect (see phylo_terms() in the data-prep chunk). pt_db_hedges_egger <- phylo_terms(db_hedges_egger, phylo_cor_hedges) # Step 1: Egger regression model with standard error as moderator egger_hedges <- metafor::rma.mv( yi = yi, V = VCV_hedges_egger, mods = ~ 1 + se, random = pt_db_hedges_egger$random, R = pt_db_hedges_egger$R, test = "t", dfs = "contain", method = "REML", sparse = TRUE, data = pt_db_hedges_egger$data ) summary(egger_hedges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 227; method: REML) logLik Deviance AIC BIC AICc -230.1194 460.2388 472.2388 492.7355 472.6242 Variance Components: estim sqrt nlvls fixed factor R sigma^2.1 0.0720 0.2683 87 no identifierStudyId no sigma^2.2 0.2635 0.5133 227 no identifierEffectSizeID no sigma^2.3 0.0000 0.0001 31 no taxonomySpecies no sigma^2.4 0.0543 0.2330 30 no species_phylo yes Test for Residual Heterogeneity: QE(df = 225) = 1287.0869, p-val < .0001 Test of Moderators (coefficient 2): F(df1 = 1, df2 = 225) = 58.4606, p-val < .0001 Model Results: estimate se tval df pval ci.lb ci.ub intrcpt -1.0341 0.2420 -4.2733 28 0.0002 -1.5298 -0.5384 *** se 4.8417 0.6332 7.6460 225 <.0001 3.5938 6.0895 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Step 2: Since the intercept is significant, re-fit using variance (vi) egger_hedges_v <- metafor::rma.mv( yi = yi, V = VCV_hedges_egger, mods = ~ 1 + vi, random = pt_db_hedges_egger$random, R = pt_db_hedges_egger$R, test = "t", dfs = "contain", method = "REML", sparse = TRUE, data = pt_db_hedges_egger$data ) summary(egger_hedges_v) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 227; method: REML) logLik Deviance AIC BIC AICc -222.7861 445.5721 457.5721 478.0687 457.9574 Variance Components: estim sqrt nlvls fixed factor R sigma^2.1 0.0532 0.2307 87 no identifierStudyId no sigma^2.2 0.2542 0.5042 227 no identifierEffectSizeID no sigma^2.3 0.0014 0.0377 31 no taxonomySpecies no sigma^2.4 0.0255 0.1597 30 no species_phylo yes Test for Residual Heterogeneity: QE(df = 225) = 1232.5374, p-val < .0001 Test of Moderators (coefficient 2): F(df1 = 1, df2 = 225) = 74.2988, p-val < .0001 Model Results: estimate se tval df pval ci.lb ci.ub intrcpt -0.2140 0.1323 -1.6179 28 0.1169 -0.4849 0.0569 vi 6.3236 0.7336 8.6197 225 <.0001 4.8779 7.7692 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: We visualize the Egger regression using a bubble plot. Effect sizes are plotted as circles scaled by precision, with the predicted regression line showing the relationship between sample size and effect size. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_egger_hedges <- orchaRd::bubble_plot( egger_hedges, mod = "se", group = "identifierStudyId", xlab = "Standard Error of Hedges' g (se)", ylab = "Effect size (Hedges' g)" ) # Color points by real source p_egger_hedges$layers[[1]]$data$real_source <- db_hedges_egger$Dataset_Source p_egger_hedges$layers[[1]]$mapping$colour <- ggplot2::aes(colour = real_source)$colour p_egger_hedges$layers[[1]]$mapping$fill <- ggplot2::aes(fill = real_source)$fill p_egger_hedges <- p_egger_hedges + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("New Extraction (Santos)" = "#D55E00", "Original (Davies 2020)" = "#0072B2"), name = "Data Source") + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("New Extraction (Santos)" = "#D55E00", "Original (Davies 2020)" = "#0072B2"), name = "Data Source") + ggplot2::ggtitle("Egger's Meta-Regression (Hedges' g)") + ggplot2::theme_minimal() print(p_egger_hedges) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](publication_bias_files/figure-html/hedges_egger_bubble_plot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: > [!NOTE] > The slope for standard error (`se`) is **positive** ($\beta = 4.84$, $SE = 0.63$, $t = 7.65$, $p < 0.0001$), indicating clear evidence of small-study effects. > > **Two-Step Correction:** The intercept of the standard error model is statistically significant ($p = 0.000$). Following the two-step recommendation of @nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022 and Stanley [-@stanleyMetaregressionAnalysisEconomics2012; -@stanleyMetaregressionApproximationsReduce2014], we re-fit Egger's regression using the sampling variance (`vi`) as the moderator. In this corrected model, the adjusted overall meta-analytic mean is estimated at $\beta_0 = -0.21$ ($SE = 0.13$, $t = -1.62$, $p = 0.117$). #### 3. Decline Effect (Time-Lag Bias) We analyze the decline effect by evaluating whether the publication year significantly predicts the effect size, while simultaneously controlling for the study sample size precision proxy. We mean-center the year so the intercept represents the effect in an average publication year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Mean-center publication year db_hedges_decline <- db_hedges_egger %>% mutate(Year_c = Year - mean(Year, na.rm = TRUE)) # VCV for decline subset VCV_hedges_decline <- metafor::vcalc(vi = vi, cluster = identifierStudyId, obs = identifierEffectSizeID, rho = 0.5, data = db_hedges_decline) # Phylogenetic random effect (see phylo_terms() in the data-prep chunk). pt_db_hedges_decline <- phylo_terms(db_hedges_decline, phylo_cor_hedges) # Time-lag decline model controlling for sampling variance (vi) decline_hedges <- metafor::rma.mv( yi = yi, V = VCV_hedges_decline, mods = ~ 1 + Year_c + vi, random = pt_db_hedges_decline$random, R = pt_db_hedges_decline$R, test = "t", dfs = "contain", method = "REML", sparse = TRUE, data = pt_db_hedges_decline$data ) summary(decline_hedges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 227; method: REML) logLik Deviance AIC BIC AICc -221.7830 443.5660 457.5660 481.4476 458.0846 Variance Components: estim sqrt nlvls fixed factor R sigma^2.1 0.0537 0.2318 87 no identifierStudyId no sigma^2.2 0.2543 0.5043 227 no identifierEffectSizeID no sigma^2.3 0.0011 0.0338 31 no taxonomySpecies no sigma^2.4 0.0357 0.1889 30 no species_phylo yes Test for Residual Heterogeneity: QE(df = 224) = 1220.7194, p-val < .0001 Test of Moderators (coefficients 2:3): F(df1 = 2, df2 = 84) = 37.4237, p-val < .0001 Model Results: estimate se tval df pval ci.lb ci.ub intrcpt -0.2186 0.1456 -1.5016 27 0.1448 -0.5172 0.0801 Year_c -0.0047 0.0064 -0.7250 84 0.4705 -0.0175 0.0081 vi 6.3534 0.7477 8.4973 224 <.0001 4.8800 7.8268 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: We construct the bubble plot showing the decline effect over years: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_decline_hedges <- orchaRd::bubble_plot( decline_hedges, mod = "Year_c", group = "identifierStudyId", xlab = "Publication Year (centered)", ylab = "Effect size (Hedges' g)" ) # Here we turn to *correcting* the pooled mean, and we directly compare two correction philosophies on the same data. * **Current method — Nakagawa et al. [-@nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022] regression correction.** We re-use the multilevel meta-regression that includes the sampling variance ($v_i$) as a moderator (the Step-2 models `egger_hedges_v` / `egger_or_v` fitted above). Its **intercept** estimates the meta-analytic mean extrapolated to $v_i = 0$ — i.e., the effect a hypothetical infinitely-precise (infinite-$n$) study would report, with the small-study component removed. This is the *"bias-corrected estimate"* in @yangRobustPointVariance2024's terminology and in `orchaRd`. * **New method — Yang et al. [-@yangRobustPointVariance2024] bias-robust estimation.** A two-step procedure: (1) fit a **multivariate fixed-/common-effect** model whose weights come from the sampling variance–covariance matrix (**FE + VCV**, assuming $\rho = 0.5$). This inverse-VCV weighting is the bias-robust ingredient: it is far less inflated by selectively-reported small studies than the random-effects mean, and it prevents studies contributing many correlated effect sizes from accumulating weight in proportion to their effect-size count. Then (2) apply **cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimation** (`clubSandwich`), clustering by study, so that standard errors and confidence intervals remain valid under the non-independence of multiple effect sizes per study. This is the *"bias-robust estimate"*. Note that the step-one model contains **no random effects**, which is why the CR2 correction is applicable here — CR2 is not valid for models with crossed random effects. We compute both, overlay them on an orchard plot of the uncorrected multilevel mean with `orchaRd::pub_bias_plot()`, and tabulate the three estimates (uncorrected vs. the two corrections) side by side. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Hedges' $g$ (Continuous outcomes) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # --- New method: Yang et al. (2024) bias-robust estimate --------------------- # Step 1: multivariate common-/fixed-effect model with the sampling # variance-covariance matrix supplying the weights ("FE + VCV"). # # The inverse-VCV weighting scheme IS the bias-robust part of the method: it # assigns smaller weights to imprecise studies reporting large effects, and it # stops a study contributing many correlated effect sizes from accumulating # weight in proportion to its effect-size count. Using rma(vi = vi) instead # would weight each effect size by 1/v_i independently, discarding the rho = # 0.5 within-study correlation assumed everywhere else in this workflow. # # rma.mv() with no `random` argument is the fixed-effect model (the fit reports # "Variance Components: none"); `method` is therefore immaterial here. VCV_hedges_fe <- metafor::vcalc( vi = vi, cluster = identifierStudyId, obs = identifierEffectSizeID, rho = 0.5, data = db_hedges_egger ) fe_hedges <- metafor::rma.mv( yi = yi, V = VCV_hedges_fe, data = db_hedges_egger, method = "REML", test = "t", dfs = "contain", sparse = TRUE ) # Step 2: cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimation, clustering by study, # to account for non-independence of multiple effect sizes per study. fe_hedges_robust <- metafor::robust( fe_hedges, cluster = db_hedges_egger$identifierStudyId, adjust = TRUE, clubSandwich = TRUE ) summary(fe_hedges_robust) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 227; method: REML) logLik Deviance AIC BIC AICc -606.7987 1213.5973 1215.5973 1219.0178 1215.6152 Variance Components: none Test for Heterogeneity: Q(df = 226) = 1389.2944, p-val < .0001 Number of estimates: 227 Number of clusters: 87 Estimates per cluster: 1-12 (mean: 2.61, median: 2) Model Results: estimate se¹ tval¹ df¹ pval¹ ci.lb¹ ci.ub¹ 0.3350 0.0438 7.6477 45.37 <.0001 0.2468 0.4232 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 1) results based on cluster-robust inference (var-cov estimator: CR2, approx t-test and confidence interval, df: Satterthwaite approx) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # `egger_hedges_v` (fitted above) is the current-method Nakagawa et al. (2022) # vi-moderator model; its intercept is the bias-corrected mean at vi = 0. ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Orchard plot of the uncorrected multilevel meta-analytic mean ... oc_hedges <- orchaRd::orchard_plot( ma_hedges, group = "identifierStudyId", xlab = "Hedges' g", angle = 0 ) # ... with both corrected means overlaid: # red = Yang et al. 2024 "Bias Robust" (fixed-effect + CR2 robust) # blue = Nakagawa et al. 2022 "Bias Corrected" (vi-moderator intercept) p_pubbias_hedges <- orchaRd::pub_bias_plot( oc_hedges, fe_model = fe_hedges_robust, v_model = egger_hedges_v ) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Bias-Corrected Means — Hedges' g") + ggplot2::theme_minimal() print(p_pubbias_hedges) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](publication_bias_files/figure-html/hedges_pub_bias_plot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: > [!NOTE] > The uncorrected multilevel mean is $\hat\mu = 0.45$ (95% CI [0.25, 0.66]). The **current** Nakagawa correction gives a bias-corrected mean of $-0.21$ (95% CI [-0.48, 0.06]), and the **new** Yang bias-robust estimate is $0.34$ (95% CI [0.25, 0.42]). ### Odds Ratio (Binary outcomes) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # --- New method: Yang et al. The **current** Nakagawa correction gives $0.10$ (95% CI [-0.23, 0.43]), and the **new** Yang bias-robust estimate is $0.55$ (95% CI [0.39, 0.71]). ::: ### Side-by-Side Comparison Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: > [!IMPORTANT] > **How to read the comparison.** Both corrections should pull the pooled estimate *toward zero* relative to the uncorrected multilevel mean if small-study/selective-reporting bias is present; the `Pct_Change_vs_Uncorrected` column quantifies that shrinkage. The two methods answer slightly different questions. The **Nakagawa** intercept is a *model-based extrapolation* to a perfectly precise study and tends to give wide confidence intervals (it is an out-of-range prediction). The **Yang** bias-robust estimate stays within the observed data, down-weights heterogeneity-driven inflation through fixed-effect weighting, and uses cluster-robust CR2 standard errors that explicitly respect the within-study dependence — making it a more conservative, inference-valid sensitivity analysis. Agreement between the two corrections strengthens confidence in the adjusted conclusion; divergence flags that the corrected mean is sensitive to modelling assumptions. --- ## Methodological Synthesis & Discussion We compile the results of the small-study effect regressions and time-lag meta-regressions for both effect size classes below: ### Publication Bias Comparison Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Main Takeaways 1. **Small-Study Effects:** The Egger's regressions indicate statistically significant small-study effects for Hedges' $g$ ($p < 0.0001$) and statistically significant small-study effects for Log Odds Ratio ($p < 0.0001$). Where present, smaller and less precise trials systematically report larger mate-choice copying effect sizes—a classic signature of publication selection, in which small-sample studies are more likely to be published or reported if they find large, hypothesis-supportive effects. 2. **Decline Effect (Time-Lag Bias) in Binary Outcomes:** The publication-year trend for binary outcomes is statistically significant ($\beta = -0.03$, $p = 0.010$). Over the last two decades, the reported strength of mate-choice copying (measured by Log Odds Ratios) has decreased, a pattern typical of fields experiencing a novelty effect in which early breakthrough publications report large effect sizes and subsequent rigorous replications reveal more moderate, realistic estimates. 3. **Time Trend in Continuous Outcomes:** For Hedges' $g$ (continuous), the publication-year trend is non-significant ($\beta = 0.00$, $p = 0.470$). This suggests the continuous reporting scales have been relatively stable in magnitude over the history of the literature. 4. **Bias-Corrected Means — Current vs. New Method:** We compared two correction frameworks on the adjusted pooled mean. For Hedges' $g$, the **current** Nakagawa [-@nakagawaMethodsTestingPublication2022] $v_i$-intercept correction yields $-0.21$ while the **new** Yang [-@yangRobustPointVariance2024] bias-robust (FE + VCV, then CR2) estimate yields $0.34$ (uncorrected multilevel mean: $0.45$). For Log Odds Ratio, the corresponding values are $0.10$ (Nakagawa) and $0.55$ (Yang), against an uncorrected mean of $0.59$. The Yang bias-robust estimate is generally the more conservative, inference-valid option because it respects within-study dependence through cluster-robust variance estimation and avoids the wide-interval extrapolation inherent in the regression-intercept approach; where the two corrections agree, the adjusted conclusion is robust to modelling choice. These diagnostic results suggest that while mate-choice copying is a genuine ecological phenomenon, the overall raw pooled estimates from both continuous and binary literatures may be moderately inflated due to selective reporting and publication biases. Future research should prioritize large-sample pre-registered replication studies to provide unbiased baselines. --- ## Session Info ::: callout-note ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sessionInfo() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) Platform: aarch64-apple-darwin23 Running under: macOS Tahoe 26.5.2 Matrix products: default BLAS: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.6/Resources/lib/libRblas.0.dylib LAPACK: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.6/Resources/lib/libRlapack.dylib;
